newsitem.title: SPAIN: Financial markets calm on Spain strike for now.
newsitem.headline: Financial markets calm on Spain strike for now.

text.p: Spain's nine-day old truckers' strike could start worrying financial markets if it lasts long enough to have an impact on prices but this looks unlikely at present, analysts said on Friday.
The government said the strike was causing serious damage to the economy but economists were confident that it would quickly find a way to resolve the dispute.
"For the moment I can't see the strike having an immediate effect on the markets," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch.
Agricultural groups estimated losses in damaged commodities so far at around 20 billion pesetas ($140 million).

Truckers have clogged major roads in most of northern Spain, cutting off supplies to factories and markets. Drivers are pressing for earlier retirement and lower diesel prices, among other conditions.
One equities dealer said the strike would be highly unlikely to endanger inflation because it would not last.

"These things are always resolved. I can't see a way that it would affect prices, because even if it went on long enough for them to tick up, prices would adjust downwards immediately that it is cleared up," he said.
"But I can't see it impacting. It hasn't occurred to anyone that it would," he added.
Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado on Friday said the economy was suffering grave damage from the strike and Spain would guarantee unimpeded travel on its roads despite the truckers' action.

"This action is conducted by a radical minority which is aiming to harm the national economy...I want to say the government will guarantee unimpeded travel on Spanish roads," he told the weekly cabinet meeting.
Some market analysts were nervous that the strike might escalate, which would be viewed badly, particular by foreign investors.
The cabinet meeting discussed alternatives to resolve the conflict.

Local press reports said truckers might be offered the possibility of paying the same diesel price as large industrial clients, which is 14 pesetas per litre less than they currently pay at petrol stations.
But petrol distribution chains are strongly opposed to this, a service stations representative told national radio.

The area hit worst by the stoppage so far is the northern Basque region and Navarre, where it is now difficult for drivers to buy petrol and perishable foods are not so readily available in local markets.
The Economy Ministry has warned that if the strike continues, prices of fruit, vegetables and fish will rise sharply.
